extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of political/social psychology; politicians and public speakers studying crowd persuasion
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts principles governing the psychology and persuasion of juries, electoral crowds, and parliamentary assemblies — what makes them decide, who influences them, and which rhetorical/organisational tactics succeed. Useful for analysing or producing political speech, campaigns, and institutional reform proposals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jury as essential protection
rubrics_metrics.description: We should cling vigorously to the jury. It constitutes, perhaps, the only category of crowd that cannot be replaced by any individuality. It alone can temper the severity of the law...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Juries provide a check on professional magistrates and can show leniency or contextual judgement (e.g., recognizing the lesser guilt of a seduced girl). Recommendation: preserve the jury as a safeguard against unchecked magistracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Origins of judicial error lie with magistrates
rubrics_metrics.description: The errors for which the jury is blamed were committed in the first instance by judges... It is solely the magistrates, then, who should be blamed when particularly monstrous judicial errors crop up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating miscarriages of justice, trace blame to prosecutorial and investigative stages (juge d'instruction, public prosecutor) rather than only to juries; reform should target magistratial procedures and oversight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jury dependence on magistrates in technical cases
rubrics_metrics.description: In all similar affairs the jury, confronted with technical details it is unable to understand, naturally hearkens to the public prosecutor, arguing that... the affair has been investigated by magistrates trained to unravel the most intricate situations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that juries defer to perceived expert authority when faced with technical evidence; therefore, managing expert testimony and prosecutorial framing heavily determines jury outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unchecked magistracy is dangerous (need for habeas corpus/control)
rubrics_metrics.description: The magistracy is... the only administration whose acts are under no control... an insignificant juge d'instruction... possesses the revolting power of sending to prison at will persons of the most considerable standing...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutional criterion: judicial investigative powers must be subject to external oversight and safeguards (habeas corpus equivalent) to prevent arbitrary detention and abuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electoral crowds: limited reasoning and high suggestibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Electoral crowds... present only a few of the characteristics previously described. Of the characteristics peculiar to crowds, they display in particular but slight aptitude for reasoning, the absence of the critical spirit, irritability, credulity, and simplicity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing electorate behaviour, expect low use of sustained argument; persuasion should target emotions, repetition, and simple appeals rather than complex reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Persuasion factors: affirmation, repetition, prestige, contagion
rubrics_metrics.description: In their decision, moreover, is to be traced the influence of the leaders of crowds and the part played by the factors we have enumerated: affirmation, repetition, prestige, and contagion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective campaigning uses repeated affirmative messages, leverages leader prestige, and creates contagious social signals (slogans, chants) rather than relying on proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Candidate must possess prestige; wealth can substitute
rubrics_metrics.description: It is of primary importance that the candidate should possess prestige. Personal prestige can only be replaced by that resulting from wealth. Talent and even genius are not elements of success of serious importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Electability metric: visible prestige (or wealth signaling) is more decisive than demonstrated talent; campaigns should invest in status-building and displays of success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flatter elector's greed and vanity; promise extravagantly
rubrics_metrics.description: The elector stickles in particular for the flattery of his greed and vanity. He must be overwhelmed with the most extravagant blandishments, and there must be no hesitation in making him the most fantastic promises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rhetorical tactic: use flattering, grandiose promises and appeals to personal interest; avoid overly cautious or modest messaging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attack rivals via affirmation and repetition without proof
rubrics_metrics.description: An effort must be made to destroy his chance by establishing by dint of affirmation, repetition, and contagion that he is an arrant scoundrel... It is, of course, useless to trouble about any semblance of proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Negative campaigning relies on repeated allegations and social amplification rather than evidentiary rebuttal; opponents who respond with reasoned arguments rather than matching affirmations lose ground.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written programme: avoid categorical pledges; verbal programme: exaggerate
rubrics_metrics.description: The candidate's written programme should not be too categorical, since later on his adversaries might bring it up against him; in his verbal programme, however, there cannot be too much exaggeration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strategic principle: keep formal/platform commitments flexible to avoid future liability, while using bold, exaggerated promises in speeches to win immediate support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power of words and formulas (magical sway of vague slogans)
rubrics_metrics.description: We shall come across them again in the action exerted by words and formulas, whose magical sway we have already insisted upon... a new formula as devoid as possible of precise meaning, and apt in consequence to flatter the most varied aspirations, infallibly obtains a success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Slogan design: favor concise, emotionally resonant phrases with broad, vague meaning so different groups can project their hopes onto them; novel formulas produce strong excitement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electioneering meetings: affirmation and invective, not argument
rubrics_metrics.description: With respect to the influence that may be exerted by reasoning on the minds of electors... In such a gathering affirmations, invectives, and sometimes blows are exchanged, but never arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect public meetings to be rhetorical and performative; organizers should plan for spectacle, managed interruptions, and the primacy of emotional rhetoric over logical debate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Election committees as central political machines and dangers
rubrics_metrics.description: "Do you know what an election committee is?... It is neither more nor less than the corner-stone of our institutions, the masterpiece of the political machine. France is governed to-day by the election committees."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organisational criterion: committees/clubs exert decisive control on votes and act as impersonal, oppressive power; assessing democratic health requires examining committee influence and patronage networks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Committees represent impersonal and oppressive tyranny
rubrics_metrics.description: Committees... constitute perhaps the most redoubtable danger resulting from the power of crowds. They represent in reality the most impersonal and, in consequence, the most oppressive form of tyranny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating democratic systems, measure the extent to which committee leaders act unaccountably in the name of collectives; centralisation of committee power is a tyranny risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universal suffrage's practical resilience despite psychological flaws
rubrics_metrics.description: I draw no conclusion against universal suffrage from what precedes. Had I to settle its fate, I should preserve it as it is for practical reasons... The dogma of universal suffrage possesses to-day the power... Time alone can act upon them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy criterion: even if mass decision-making is flawed psychologically, altering suffrage may not improve outcomes because crowd-leveling effects persist and democratic dogma is entrenched.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition of electorate does not substantially change crowd decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Were the electorate solely composed of persons stuffed with sciences their votes would be no better than those emitted at present... In a crowd men always tend to the same level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reform implication: restricting franchise to supposedly 'better' individuals is unlikely to yield better collective decisions; crowd dynamics tend to equalize judgments regardless of individual education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parliamentary assemblies share crowd traits but are non-anonymous
rubrics_metrics.description: In parliamentary assemblies we have an example of heterogeneous crowds that are not anonymous... they present very similar characteristics... the influence of the race makes itself felt to weaken or exaggerate the characteristics common to crowds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analysing legislative behaviour, account for crowd effects (suggestibility, simplicity) combined with identifiable leaders and institutional constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assemblies display intellectual simplicity and tendency to dogmatism
rubrics_metrics.description: Simplicity in their opinions is one of their most important characteristics... an invariable tendency... to solve the most complicated social problems by the simplest abstract principles and general laws applicable to all cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect legislative debate to simplify complex problems into broad dogmas; policy messaging should therefore use simple, memorable principles to sway assemblies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fixed local/regional opinions resist argument
rubrics_metrics.description: On all questions of local or regional interest every member of an assembly has fixed, unalterable opinions, which no amount of argument can shake.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Electoral/constituency pressures create entrenched positions; persuasive efforts on such matters are unlikely to change votes — alternative strategies (coalitions, incentives) are needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: General questions: indecision and shifting under competing leaders
rubrics_metrics.description: On general questions... there is no longer any fixity of opinion, and the suggestions of leaders can exert an influence... The Deputy finds himself placed between two contrary suggestions, and is inevitably made to hesitate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For broad national issues, leader competition produces volatility; timing and signalling by leaders can decisively swing outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leaders' power derives from prestige, not argument
rubrics_metrics.description: The influence of the leaders is due in very small measure to the arguments they employ, but in a large degree to their prestige... should they... lose their prestige, their influence disappears.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leadership effectiveness is primarily about perceived prestige and authority; cultivating prestige (symbolic acts, reputation management) is more impactful than refining arguments alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oratorical art: energetic affirmations, impressive images, summary arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: He should possess a special description of eloquence, composed of energetic affirmations--unburdened with proofs-- and impressive images, accompanied by very summary arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Speechcraft guideline: use bold statements, vivid imagery, and concise supporting points rather than lengthy proofs; striking phrasing dominates in assemblies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of striking terms and exaggerated declamation to intimidate dissent
rubrics_metrics.description: Too much importance cannot be attached to the 'striking terms'... The affirmation is never too violent, the declamation never too threatening. Nothing intimidates the audience more than this sort of eloquence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rhetorical tactic: employ dramatic, intimidating language to silence or deter opposition; escalate rhetoric in moments of crisis for maximal effect (ethical and legal implications aside).

rubrics_metrics.name: Intelligence can reduce a leader's persuasive power
rubrics_metrics.description: By showing how complex things are, by allowing of explanation and promoting comprehension, intelligence always renders its owner indulgent, and blunts, in a large measure, that intensity and violence of conviction needful for apostles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paradox: highly analytical, explanatory speakers may fail to mobilize crowds; rhetorical simplicity and conviction often trump nuanced expertise in leadership contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specialists influence technical questions, mitigating crowd effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Cases in which an assembly loses the characteristics of crowds--The influence of specialists when technical questions arise--The advantages and dangers of a parliamentary system...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When debates turn technical, specialist knowledge can override general crowd tendencies; policy design should allocate technical matters to experts to reduce populist simplification.
